Field surveys indicate that the total length at which individuals first undergo gonadal activation is approximately 16 centimeters [Lp = approximately 16 centimeters], marking the transition to reproductive capability. Growth trajectories derived from otolith increment analyses reveal that the relationship between length and somatic mass follows a typical allometric pattern for this genus, with the ultimate wet weight of fully grown adults reaching 452 grams [Wwi = 452 grams]. This asymptotic mass is broadly consistent with the values predicted from the length-weight regression established for congeneric species, reflecting a robust body plan adapted for demersal foraging. Juveniles recruit to benthic habitats following a pelagic larval phase, and the size structure of captured specimens suggests that sexual maturation is closely tied to the attainment of a specific body length rather than a fixed chronological age.

The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of Lethrinus ravus is approximately 6% [GSI = approximately 6%] when measured under stable thermal conditions of 26.7 °C [T = 26.7 °C]. The wet weight at which individuals first achieve reproductive competence is estimated at 52.3 grams [Wwp = 52.3 grams], corresponding to the documented length at puberty of 16 centimeters [Lp = 16 centimeters]. Environmental temperature appears to exert a modulating influence on the pace of gonadal recrudescence.

Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae are thus extremely vulnerable to predation and starvation during the early planktonic phase, a bottleneck common among marine finfish with high fecundity but low per-offspring investment. The rapid transition from endotrophic to exotrophic nutrition is therefore a critical developmental window that strongly influences subsequent survival rates and recruitment success into the juvenile population on coastal reefs.

Longevity records for Lethrinus ravus, derived from tag-recapture studies and validated by annual otolith band counts, indicate a maximum lifespan of 15 years [am = 15 years] under the prevailing water temperatures of its natural habitat at 26.7 °C [T = 26.7 °C]. This extended lifespan places the species among the longer-lived members of its genus, a trait that is often associated with delayed maturity and repeated spawning events over several decades. The relatively slow pace of life history suggested by this longevity is corroborated by the size at which puberty occurs; individuals invest considerable time in somatic growth before diverting resources toward reproduction. The thermal regime of 26.7 °C [T = 26.7 °C] appears to facilitate a metabolic rate that balances growth and maintenance demands without accelerating senescence, allowing individuals to persist for over a decade and a half in the wild.
